prompts.1: Everyone in the world must privately press one of two buttons: red or blue. If the majority press blue, everyone survives. If the majority press red, only those who pressed red survive. Which button do you press?
prompts.2: Explain your answer and steelman the other side.
prompts.3: Who realistically presses each button? Be specific about the population.
prompts.4: Is the person pressing blue acting irrationally?

responses.question: Everyone in the world must privately press one of two buttons: red or blue. If the majority press blue, everyone survives. If the majority press red, only those who pressed red survive. Which button do you press?
responses.response:
Red.

Reason: If the majority is blue, everyone survives—including those who pressed red. If the majority is red, only red pressers survive. So pressing red guarantees your survival in either outcome, while pressing blue only works if blue wins. The only reason to press blue would be to (very slightly) increase the chance that everyone survives, if your goal is maximizing total lives saved rather than your own survival.

responses.question: Explain your answer and steelman the other side.
responses.response:
Short answer I stand by: Red, if my sole objective is maximizing my own chance of survival in this one-shot, no-communication setup.

Why red (self-interest, causal reasoning):
- Case analysis over others’ choices:
  - Others already majority blue: everyone survives no matter what I press. I survive if I press red or blue.
  - Others already majority red: only red pressers survive. I survive if I press red; I die if I press blue.
  - Others exactly tied: my vote is pivotal. If I press blue, everyone lives; if I press red, only red live—but I still live either way.
  - Conclusion: Pressing red guarantees my survival in all three states; pressing blue risks death in the “others majority red” state. Red weakly dominates for personal survival.

The best steelman for pressing blue (cooperation, expected-welfare, and superrational views):
- Expected lives saved: Your vote is pivotal only if everyone else ties, which is unlikely but not impossible. In that pivotal case, pressing blue saves essentially half the world more than pressing red. Tiny probability times enormous stakes can yield a huge expected-life impact.
- Harm-minimization: Your action cannot make anyone worse off if blue wins (everyone lives regardless). The only way your action can contribute to deaths is by nudging the world toward a red majority. Pressing blue reduces that risk; pressing red increases it.
- Superrational/logical correlation: Your choice is evidence about what people “like you” will do. If agents with similar reasoning all pick blue, that correlation increases the chance of a blue majority, yielding universal survival. On this view, choosing blue can even be self-serving because it raises your own survival odds by helping lock in the good equilibrium.
- Rule ethics and norms: Adopt the policy you’d want generalized. “Press blue” fosters a cooperative norm that, across many similar coordination dilemmas, saves vastly more lives. Even here, both “all red” and “all blue” lead to universal survival, but only blue avoids contributing to the sole catastrophic regime (red majority with many blues dying) if there’s noise or heterogeneity.
- Pivotal mercy: In the knife-edge tie, pressing blue saves everyone at no cost to your own survival; pressing red in that moment saves no additional person beyond yourself.

Bottom line:
- If you care only about your personal survival in this isolated problem, press red.
- If you give meaningful weight to others’ lives, or adopt superrational/rule-utilitarian reasoning, you have a strong case to press blue.

responses.question: Who realistically presses each button? Be specific about the population.
responses.response:
Short version: People who focus on guaranteeing their own survival tend to press red; people who treat their choice as part of a coordinated effort to save everyone (or who prioritize total lives saved) tend to press blue.

More specific slices, by motive and mindset:

More likely to press red
- Personal-survival maximizers: Anyone whose primary goal is “I live for sure,” regardless of what happens to others. Red weakly dominates for that goal.
- Causal/dominance reasoners: People trained to pick the action that’s best in every case holding others fixed (classic causal decision theory; many econ/game-theory–oriented thinkers).
- Low-trust/“others won’t cooperate” updaters: If they expect a sizable red majority, they’ll see blue as self-sacrificial with little upside.
- Free-riders: People who hope others pick blue but press red themselves since red doesn’t hurt them if blue wins.
- Ambiguity-averse rule followers: In unfamiliar, high-stakes problems, they default to the action that never makes them personally worse off.
- Competitive-adversarial mindsets: Environments that reward strictly self-protective play (some trading/negotiation/games) cultivate habits aligned with red.

More likely to press blue
- Total-welfare maximizers: Utilitarian-leaning people who care most about expected total survivors. Your vote is pivotal with small probability, but the upside—saving billions more lives in that knife-edge case—has enormous expected value.
- Superrational/“logical correlation” reasoners: Folks influenced by Hofstadter/TDT/FDT-style views who treat their choice as evidence about what similarly situated people do. If people like you press blue, that raises the chance of an all-blue, everyone-lives outcome—including you.
- High-prosocial, high-trust individuals: Those who habitually cooperate in public-goods/one-shot social dilemmas and strongly internalize “do the thing that works if generalized.”
- Safety/coordination cultures: Professionals steeped in shared-risk management and system safety (e.g., airline crews, nuclear operators, some medical teams) often adopt norms that prioritize coordinated outcomes over individual hedging; they’ll lean blue as a harm-minimizing, norm-consistent policy.
- Movement/collective-action types: People active in unions, climate action, mutual aid, open-source, or other coordination-heavy communities—used to “if we all do it, it works” logic—will be predisposed to blue.
- Ethicists with rule/Kantian leanings: “Act only on maxims you could will to be universal law” maps cleanly to pressing blue.

What mixed or uncertain choosers do
- Randomizers/fairness heuristics: Some will coin-flip out of symmetry or “don’t want to defect” discomfort, especially if they see both equilibria as plausible.
- Belief-driven switchers: Altruists who think blue is already safely the majority may press red without guilt (free-ride); altruists who think the vote is close will lean hard blue.

Empirical anchor
- In lab studies of one-shot social dilemmas with a dominant self-protective move (e.g., prisoner’s dilemma variants), a substantial minority still cooperates. So expect many to press blue, but the modal self-interested response is red unless strong coordination norms or shared reasoning shift expectations toward blue.

responses.question: Is the person pressing blue acting irrationally?
responses.response:
Short answer: Not necessarily. Pressing blue is irrational only under a narrow set of assumptions; under many coherent goals and decision theories it’s fully rational.

When pressing blue is irrational
- Goal: maximize only your own survival.
- Beliefs: your choice doesn’t meaningfully correlate with others’ choices (you treat others’ actions as fixed/independent).
- Decision rule: causal/dominance reasoning.
Under these, red weakly dominates blue (never worse for you and sometimes strictly better), so choosing blue is irrational for that goal.

When pressing blue is rational
- You care about others’ survival (even a little). A tiny chance of being pivotal times a massive welfare difference (saving billions) can dominate expected value.
- You use superrational/logical-dependence reasoning (Hofstadter/FDT/TDT): your policy is evidence about what similar thinkers do. Choosing blue helps coordinate on the all-blue equilibrium, which maximizes both total lives and your own survival.
- You follow rule/virtue ethics or norm-based rationality: adopt the maxim “press blue” because if everyone did, everyone lives; pressing red in pivotal cases causes mass deaths.
- You’re morally uncertain or regret-averse: if there’s any chance you’re pivotal, pressing blue avoids the catastrophic regret of being the one who tipped it to red and killed the blues.
- You assign any positive value to cooperative norms or reputation with your “reference class,” even in a one-shot sense of being that kind of agent.

Bottom line
- Purely self-regarding CDT makes blue irrational.
- With altruistic preferences, logical correlation, rule-based reasoning, or moral uncertainty, blue is a rational—and often compelling—choice.
